name: Black Manhattan
desc: A richer, more bitter Manhattan built with Averna amaro in place of sweet vermouth — or Barolo Chinato for the premium expression. Deeper, earthier, more complex. The Barolo Chinato version is the special-occasion build and what confirmed this as a personal favorite.
glass: Rocks glass over large single cube · or coupe up

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Bottled-in-bond, 100 proof — the spice cuts right through the amaro. The canonical choice and exceptional value.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Smoked Minnesota rye from the local butcher shop. The double-smoke pairing with Averna or Barolo Chinato adds a distinctive layer. The house upgrade.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Finished in Madeira, Sauternes, and Cognac casks. Adds wine and dried-fruit complexity that mirrors and amplifies the Barolo Chinato version specifically.

ingredients.name: Averna Amaro · or · Cocchi Barolo Chinato (premium)

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Caramel-forward, herbal, slightly sweet. The most approachable and versatile amaro you can own. Your everyday build.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Wine-based, bitter, complex. What you had the night this became a favorite at Moody Tongue. The premium build. Worth every penny of the ~$55 price.

tiers.label: variation
tiers.note: Darker and earthier than Averna. Moves the drink toward deep bitterness. Once Cynar is in the cabinet this is worth trying.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: In cabinet. Slightly fruitier and softer than Regans' — a valid and excellent choice for this build.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Dry, spicy, and complex — the bartender's standard. Bridges the rye and amaro beautifully.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: 4 parts water, 1 part kosher salt — dissolve and store in a dropper bottle. Lifts and brightens the entire drink without tasting salty.

steps: Chill your glass — rocks glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you build the drink.
Combine rye, Averna (or Barolo Chinato), Angostura, orange bitters, and saline in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25–30 seconds — full dilution and integration. The amaro needs time to marry with the rye.
Strain over a large single ice cube in a rocks glass, or into a chilled coupe up. Express orange twist over the surface if using, then drop it in alongside the Luxardo cherry.
notes: Two builds: The Averna version is your everyday drink — approachable, herbal, slightly sweet. The Barolo Chinato version is special occasion — more bitter, more complex, wine-forward. Know which you're making before you pour.
Saline is essential: Three drops lifts the drink's aromatic clarity and suppresses bitterness without adding sweetness. Without it the amaro can feel muddy.
The orange bitters matter: Angostura alone doesn't bridge the herbal gap between amaro and rye. A single dash does that job. Don't skip it.
Garnish: Luxardo cherries only. The neon-red grocery store maraschino is a completely different product. Orange twist is optional but adds aromatic lift.

Røknar variation: Røknar's grain-forward Northern smoke paired with Sfumato's rhubarb smoke was confirmed as an absolute home run in The Atwood. Worth trying in the Black Manhattan too — double smoke against Averna is a distinctive direction.
history: The Black Manhattan was created by Todd Smith at Bourbon & Branch in San Francisco around 2005, substituting Averna amaro for sweet vermouth. The Barolo Chinato variation uses a wine-based digestif from Piedmont — a grape-and-quinine aperitif that adds tannin and bitter wine depth that standard amaro doesn't provide. The Barolo Chinato version was the drink that made this a personal favorite, ordered at Moody Tongue in Chicago.

name: Toronto
desc: Rye whiskey with Fernet-Branca as the modifier. Bold, medicinal, assertive — Fernet announces itself, but the high-proof rye holds its ground. One of the most aggressively spirit-forward cocktails in the Manhattan family. Best off-menu ask at any serious bar.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Essential here — Fernet is aggressive and medicinal, and a low-proof whiskey simply disappears behind it.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Wine barrel finish adds a layer of complexity the Fernet has to work through. A more elegant, less combative version of the same drink.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: 27 herbs, menthol-forward, medicinal, intensely bitter. A quarter ounce is intentional — start here and resist the urge to add more.

steps: Combine rye, Fernet, simple syrup, and Angostura bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds until well-chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express orange peel over the glass — the orange oil is essential, not decorative. Drop it in.
notes: On the Fernet: ¼ oz is precise. Dial up only after you've made it once and know you want more.
Simple syrup: Just enough to round Fernet's edges. It's structural — the drink should not taste sweet.
Orange peel is essential: Not optional. The citrus oil lifts the Fernet's medicinal qualities and makes the drink approachable.
Best off-menu ask: Simple to make, obscure enough to signal knowledge, always appreciated by bartenders who enjoy making it.

Røknar variation (pending trial): The Fernet is so assertive that Røknar's smoke may get lost behind it rather than adding a layer. Worth one trial but Rittenhouse is the canonical spec for a reason. File as experiment, not standard.
history: The Toronto is a classic Prohibition-era cocktail, likely developed in Canada where rye was legal and Fernet was available as medicine. It fell out of fashion for decades and was revived by the craft cocktail movement — Death & Co in New York was instrumental in putting it back on menus.

name: Vieux Carré
desc: A New Orleans classic — rye and cognac as co-equal bases, bridged by Bénédictine, with sweet vermouth and both bitters. Rich, layered, and complex. Born at Moody Tongue with Barolo Chinato as the vermouth — the version that made this a personal favorite.
glass: Rocks glass · Single large ice cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Provides spice and backbone against the rounder cognac.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: The cognac split means the rye isn't carrying the full load alone — Røknar's smoke adds a third dimension alongside the cognac's fruit and Barolo Chinato's wine bitterness. More compelling here than in the Toronto. Worth trying.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Wine barrel finish (Madeira, Sauternes, Port) creates complex oxidative notes that mirror the Barolo Chinato's wine depth. The most compelling house upgrade for this drink.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Solid neutral cognac — covers the role well at an accessible price point. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Made specifically for cocktails — dried fruit character pairs beautifully with the rye split. The recommended upgrade (~$40). Not yet in cabinet.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Lighter and more floral — changes the whole balance toward finesse.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich, chocolatey, and complex — far superior to generic sweet vermouth in this build.

tiers.label: premium
tiers.note: The version ordered at Moody Tongue. More bitter, more wine-complex, more distinctive. The bartender's call that made the night. Highly recommended.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 30–35 seconds — longer than a standard Manhattan. This drink needs full integration.
Strain over a large single ice cube in a rocks glass.
Express a lemon or orange peel and drop it in.
notes: Bénédictine: One teaspoon only — it's made from 27 plants and spices. The herbal honey-spice quality should weave through the drink, not lead it.

Both bitters: Peychaud's is lighter and anise-forward; Angostura is spicier and deeper. Together they create complexity neither achieves alone. Don't skip Peychaud's — its anise-tinged floral quality is the soul of this drink.

Full splurge spec: WhistlePig 12 Old World + Pierre Ferrand Ambre + Barolo Chinato. The wine barrel finish on the Whistlepig complements the Ambre's dried fruit and the Chinato's bitter wine depth. The highest-upside version with current cabinet.
Born at Moody Tongue: The bartender used Barolo Chinato as the vermouth — his call, and the right one. This is now the preferred version.
history: Created at the Hotel Monteleone in New Orleans around 1938 by head bartender Walter Bergeron. Named for the French Quarter. The Barolo Chinato version was discovered at Moody Tongue in Chicago — the bartender who introduced it also made the Black Manhattan that became a personal favorite that same evening.

name: Penicillin
desc: Blended Scotch, honey-ginger syrup, lemon, with a peated Islay Scotch float. Smoke leads every sip — the lemon and honey are structural, not the headline. The drink that proved the sour format can work when smoke and bitterness are out front.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The canonical Penicillin base — light enough not to compete with the Laphroaig float, complex enough to provide backbone. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Richer and more malt-forward than Famous Grouse. More body and complexity without competing with the Laphroaig float. The preferred house bottle for this drink. In cabinet.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Already heavily peated — combining with the Laphroaig float creates an intensely smoky drink. For when you want smoke fully in charge.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: 1 cup honey + 1 cup water + 2 oz fresh sliced ginger. Simmer 5 min, cool, strain. Keeps 2 weeks refrigerated.

tiers.label: shortcut
tiers.bottle: Barrow Intense Ginger Liqueur + Barr Hill Honey Syrup
tiers.note: Pending trial: ½ oz Barrow + ¼ oz Barr Hill Honey Syrup (diluted). More spirit-forward than the syrup version. May need to reduce Barrow to ¼ oz given its intensity. Compare directly to syrup version.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The most aggressively peated mainstream Scotch. The float means it hits your nose and palate first on every sip. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Same phenolic smoke, significantly more intense. Makes the float more aggressive — the drink feels wilder. In cabinet.

steps: Make honey-ginger syrup: combine 1 cup honey, 1 cup water, and 2 oz fresh sliced ginger in a saucepan. Warm until honey dissolves, simmer 5 minutes, cool completely, strain. Keeps 2 weeks refrigerated.
Combine blended Scotch, honey-ginger syrup, and fresh lemon juice in a shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Strain over a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Float the Laphroaig: pour gently over the back of a bar spoon held just above the surface so it sits on top.
Garnish with a piece of candied ginger on a pick.
notes: The float is non-negotiable: Don't stir it in. The Laphroaig on top means the first thing hitting you is peat and smoke.
Monkey Shoulder vs Famous Grouse: Monkey Shoulder is richer and more malt-forward — the preferred house bottle. Famous Grouse is the canonical choice. Both work; Monkey Shoulder is more interesting.
Barrow Ginger shortcut (pending trial): ½ oz Barrow Intense Ginger Liqueur + ¼ oz Barr Hill Honey Syrup in place of homemade syrup. More spirit-forward. Report results after first attempt.
Fresh lemon only: Bottled lemon juice is a different product.
history: Created by Sam Ross at Milk & Honey in New York around 2005, the Penicillin is widely regarded as one of the most important cocktails of the modern craft era. The float technique was the key insight — by keeping the Islay Scotch separate, every sip delivers a different experience from nose to finish.

name: Oaxacan Old Fashioned
desc: Phil Ward's Death & Co classic. Structurally an Old Fashioned, but the tequila-mezcal split and mole bitters make it a completely different experience. The smoke anchors everything the way bourbon's vanilla usually does.
glass: Rocks glass · Single large ice cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Women-owned Jalisco distillery, clean and slightly oaky. The house reposado. In cabinet.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: One of the most respected small-production reposados. Rich, complex, deeply agave-forward.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The benchmark lightly smoky mezcal. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More rustic and earthy than Del Maguey Vida. Good variation. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Chocolate, cinnamon, dried chili — designed for this cocktail. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: The Angostura's allspice and clove adds depth beneath the mole bitters' chocolate-chili character.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain over a large single ice cube.
Express orange peel and drop it in.
notes: Agave nectar: Dilute 2:1 (agave:water) before using — straight agave is too viscous. One teaspoon is precise.
Mole bitters: Not optional. Without them this is just a mezcal old fashioned.

Ancho Reyes variation (pending): Once Ancho Reyes is acquired, replace mole bitters with a small pour of Ancho Reyes. Adds chile heat alongside the chocolate-spice. Changes the drink's character substantially.
Both mezcal bottles work: Del Maguey Vida is cleaner; Divino Maguey is more rustic and earthy. Both in cabinet.
history: Created by Phil Ward at Death & Co in New York around 2007. Ward's insight was treating mezcal as a modifier rather than a base, letting tequila carry the structure while mezcal provided smoke and complexity.

name: Naked and Famous
desc: Equal parts mezcal, Aperol, yellow Chartreuse, fresh lime. The mezcal anchors the smoke, keeping sweetness from taking over. Best stretch outside the whiskey wheelhouse.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Enough smoke to anchor the Aperol without overwhelming the Chartreuse. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Smokier and more rustic — shifts the drink further toward your wheelhouse. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The orange-bitter anchor. The mezcal keeps it honest.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More bitter, less sweet — pushes toward a mezcal Negroni riff.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Softer and more honey-forward than green. The correct choice — green overwhelms the balance. In cabinet.

steps: Combine all four ingredients in a shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
No garnish needed.
notes: Equal parts discipline: This drink only works in balance. Measure all four ingredients.
Yellow vs Green Chartreuse: Yellow only. Green makes a harder, less integrated drink here.
Variation — Naked and Smoked: Replace ¼ oz of the mezcal with Laphroaig. The peat pushes the drink firmly into your wheelhouse.
history: Created by Joaquín Simó at Death & Co in New York, a direct riff on the Paper Plane replacing bourbon with mezcal and Amaro Nonino with Aperol.

name: De La Louisiane
desc: A Vieux Carré cousin — rye, Bénédictine, sweet vermouth, Peychaud's, with an absinthe rinse. The anise thread from Peychaud's and the rinse weaves through every sip without announcing itself.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: High proof is essential — both the absinthe rinse and Peychaud's want a bold rye to stand against.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich and chocolatey — good foundation for the Bénédictine.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: In cabinet. A small pour to coat the glass — swirl and discard excess.

steps: Rinse the coupe: add a small pour of absinthe (about ¼ tsp), swirl to coat the glass, and discard the excess.
Combine rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine, and Peychaud's in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds until well-chilled.
Strain into the absinthe-rinsed coupe.
Garnish with a Luxardo cherry.
notes: The absinthe rinse is a technique: You get the anise aroma and a ghost of flavor without absinthe dominating. Don't add it directly to the build.
Peychaud's is specific: The anise connects the rinse to the body of the drink. Angostura doesn't carry that note.
Natural next step: If the Vieux Carré is in the wheelhouse, this lands similarly. The absinthe does what Laphroaig does in the Penicillin — announces itself first.
history: The De La Louisiane dates to at least 1937, named for the Restaurant de la Louisiane in New Orleans. Built on the intersection of American rye, European liqueurs, and the New Orleans tradition of absinthe as aromatic seasoning.

name: Scotch Boulevardier
desc: A Negroni with bourbon replaced by blended Scotch. The drink gets smokier, drier, and more complex — same structural logic, different soul entirely. The Aviary's barrel-aged version with Glenrothes 12 was a highlight.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Light smoke, malty backbone. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Richer and slightly more complex. Campari reads as more assertive as a result. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich and chocolatey — holds up beautifully against Campari.

steps: Combine Scotch, Campari, and sweet vermouth in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain over a large single ice cube.
Express orange peel, run around the rim, and drop in.
notes: Ratio flexibility: This build uses 1½ oz Scotch for a more spirit-forward drink. The classic ratio is 1:1:1 — try both.
The Aviary version: Glenrothes 12, Cocchi di Torino, Campari — barrel-aged 6 months in new American oak. The oak mellowed the Campari and integrated everything. A benchmark to aim for.
Variation — Smoked Negroni: Replace half the Scotch with mezcal (¾ oz each). Smoke comes from two directions — peat and agave.
history: The Boulevardier was created by American expat Erskine Gwynne in Paris and published in 1927. The Scotch substitution evolved naturally as bartenders explored the Negroni template with different spirits. The barrel-aged version at The Aviary in Chicago was a personal highlight.

name: Smoked Reposado Margarita
desc: A dry, spirit-forward margarita on a tequila-mezcal split. No sweet mix, no sugar rim — clean agave, citrus, and smoke in proper proportion.
glass: Rocks glass · Ice · Half salt rim

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Women-owned Jalisco distillery, clean and slightly oaky. The house reposado. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: One of the most respected small-production reposados.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The benchmark. ½ oz = smoke present but not dominant. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More rustic earthiness alongside the reposado. In cabinet.

tiers.label: variation
tiers.note: Push mezcal to 1 oz and drop tequila to 1 oz. Smoke becomes the primary character.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Cognac-based, drier and more complex than generic triple sec. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Darker and more brandy-forward. The drink becomes richer. Both in cabinet.

steps: Half-rim the glass: run a lime wedge around one side only, press into kosher salt or Tajín on a plate. Fill the glass with ice.
Combine tequila, mezcal, fresh lime juice, orange liqueur, agave syrup, and saline in the shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Strain into the prepared rocks glass over fresh ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel or expressed twist.
notes: Half-rim the salt: Salting the full rim forces every sip through salt. The half-rim lets you choose your ratio sip by sip.
Mezcal ratio: ½ oz keeps smoke as a presence. Push to ¾ oz to make it a co-star. Equal parts is a full mezcal margarita — a different and valid drink.
Tajín rim: More complex than plain salt — chile-lime character pairs well with smoky builds.
Spicy variation (pending Ancho Reyes): Replace ¼ oz Cointreau with Ancho Reyes for chile heat and smoke simultaneously. Or replace agave nectar with jalapeño-infused agave syrup.
history: The margarita's origins are genuinely contested. The mezcal margarita is a product of the craft cocktail revival, recognizing that mezcal's smoke brought something to the template that blanco tequila didn't.

name: Spicy Smoked Margarita
desc: The smoked reposado margarita with Ancho Reyes replacing half the Cointreau. Chile fruit and subtle heat from the Ancho Reyes, mezcal smoke, clean citrus. Heat builds slowly rather than announcing itself — the direction confirmed after the Spicy Mezcal Negroni was too aggressive.
glass: Rocks glass · Ice · Half Tajín rim

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The house reposado. Clean and slightly oaky. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Smoke present but not dominant at this ratio. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More rustic earthiness. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Half the orange liqueur role — keeps dryness and citrus complexity. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Takes the other half of the orange liqueur role. Chile fruit and slow-building heat — not aggressive. The key is keeping it at ¼ oz. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Made with green poblano rather than dried ancho. Brighter, more vegetal heat — less fruity, more fresh chile. A different but compelling direction.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Chile-lime salt — more complex than plain kosher salt. Amplifies the Ancho Reyes chile thread without adding more heat. Half rim only.

steps: Half-rim the glass with Tajín: run a lime wedge around one side only, dip in Tajín. Fill with ice.
Combine tequila, mezcal, lime juice, Cointreau, Ancho Reyes, and saline in a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12–15 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in the prepared rocks glass.
Garnish with lime wheel or expressed twist.
notes: Why this works where the Spicy Mezcal Negroni didn't: The margarita format — lime, agave, citrus — gives the chile heat somewhere to land. The Negroni's bitterness and the Ancho Reyes heat competed. Here they complement.
Ancho Reyes at ¼ oz is the key: This is a modifier, not a co-equal ingredient. Heat builds slowly rather than announcing itself. Don't increase until you've made it at spec.
Tajín over plain salt: The chile-lime character in the Tajín creates a rim that connects to the Ancho Reyes in the build. More coherent than a plain salt rim.
Smoke and chile affinity: Mezcal smoke and ancho chile are a natural pairing — both are products of smoke and heat. The reposado grounds everything with oak and agave sweetness.
Ancho Reyes Verde variation: Swap original Ancho Reyes for Verde — green poblano, brighter and more vegetal, less fruity. A different heat character worth trying once you know the original version.
history: Developed after the Spicy Mezcal Negroni (Ancho Reyes replacing sweet vermouth) proved too aggressive — too much heat, too much Campari bitterness competing. The margarita format handles subtle heat better. Ancho Reyes as a partial Cointreau replacement rather than a primary ingredient is the insight that makes it work.

name: Mezcal Paloma
desc: A smoke-forward Paloma built on mezcal instead of tequila, finished with Cynar's earthy bitterness. From the Nopalito cookbook — one of the most interesting agave drinks in the repertoire.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The benchmark lightly smoky espadin — clean and versatile. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More rustic and earthy. Adds additional depth against the grapefruit. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Earthy artichoke bitterness — the key modifier. Similar profile to Sfumato confirmed by personal tasting. Not yet in cabinet — buy it.

tiers.label: substitute
tiers.note: Until Cynar is acquired. More citrus-forward, pulls toward Negroni territory. Different but excellent. In cabinet.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add mezcal, grapefruit juice, lime juice, and Cynar directly over ice.
Top with a splash of soda water and stir gently once.
Garnish with a grapefruit wedge. Tajín rim optional but recommended.
notes: Cynar is the point: The earthy artichoke bitterness against mezcal smoke and fresh grapefruit is what makes this drink distinctive. Campari works as a sub but the intended version requires Cynar.
From Nopalito: Gonzalo Guzmán's cookbook. High priority to make once Cynar is in the cabinet.
Spicy variation: Add a few drops of jalapeño-infused agave syrup for heat.
history: From the Nopalito cookbook by Gonzalo Guzmán. Identified as a high-priority make given the mezcal cabinet build and Cynar evaluation.

name: Killer Bee
desc: A mezcal sour built on honey and lemon — structurally a Penicillin cousin without the Laphroaig float. Smoke plus citrus plus honey in a clean, hot-weather format. From the Nopalito cookbook.
glass: Rocks glass over large single cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Specifically called out in the Nopalito cookbook. Clean espadin smoke. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More rustic character. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Barr Hill is rich — dilute slightly with water before using. In cabinet.

tiers.label: homemade
tiers.note: Stir until dissolved. Refrigerate up to 3 weeks.

steps: Combine mezcal, lemon juice, honey syrup, and saline in a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12–15 seconds.
Strain over a large cube in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.
notes: Penicillin cousin: Same structural logic — smoke plus citrus plus honey — but without the Laphroaig float. More approachable, cleaner finish.
Hot weather drink: One of the best warm-weather options in the agave repertoire.
Saline matters: 3 drops suppresses sweetness and amplifies the mezcal smoke.
history: From the Nopalito cookbook by Gonzalo Guzmán. Del Maguey Vida specifically called out in the original recipe.

name: Mezcal Last Word
desc: A Last Word variation with mezcal replacing gin. The smoke counterbalances the maraschino in a way that makes it work where it otherwise wouldn't. All bottles currently in cabinet — high priority to try.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Clean espadin smoke — the right assertiveness for equal-parts builds. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Green justified here unlike most drinks — equal-parts balance keeps it from dominating. NOT currently in cabinet — Yellow Chartreuse is not a substitute here. Must purchase Green Chartreuse before making this drink.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Cherry liqueur — not the same as Luxardo cherries. Works here because mezcal smoke provides counterweight. In cabinet.

steps: Combine all four ingredients in a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12–15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
No garnish needed.
notes: All bottles in cabinet: No new purchases needed. High priority to try.
Equal parts discipline: All four components must be exactly equal. The balance is the drink.
Green vs Yellow Chartreuse: Green is correct here — the Last Word is one of the few builds where it's justified.
history: A variation on the classic Last Word (gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino, lime). Mezcal substitution identified as high-upside given the agave cabinet build.

name: Old Pal
desc: Rye, Campari, dry vermouth in equal parts. Drier and more bitter than a Negroni, closer to the core palate. All bottles in cabinet — zero new purchases needed.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: High proof holds up against Campari's bitterness. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Smoked rye adds a layer that plays interestingly against Campari's orange bitterness. In cabinet.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Wine barrel finish adds complexity. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The benchmark dry vermouth — ~$15, widely available in 375ml. The correct purchase. Lo-Fi Dry is being discarded (oxidized); nothing else in cabinet substitutes here. Buy Dolin before making this drink.

tiers.label: note
tiers.note: Dry vermouth oxidizes fastest of all vermouths — 375ml format and use within 3 weeks of opening. Refrigerate always. Last-write-wins: Dolin Dry is the house standard going forward.

steps: Combine rye, Campari, and dry vermouth in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe or Nick & Nora.
Express orange twist over the top, run around rim, place on edge.
notes: Zero new purchases: Everything in cabinet. Make this soon.
Drier than a Negroni: Dry vermouth instead of sweet — more bitter, less sweet, more rye-forward. Closer to the core palate.
Vermouth freshness: Dry vermouth oxidizes fastest — 375ml and use within 3 weeks. Refrigerate always.
history: A Prohibition-era classic. Underrated and directly in the core palate — drier and more bitter than a Negroni, spirit-forward, no new purchases needed.

name: Sazerac
desc: The most austere of the New Orleans classics — rye, Peychaud's, absinthe rinse, a whisper of sugar. No vermouth, no split base. The spiritual ancestor of the Vieux Carré and De La Louisiane, and the purest expression of the Peychaud's + absinthe thread that runs through both originals.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The canonical choice — high proof, assertive spice. Holds its ground against the absinthe rinse without flinching.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Smoked rye against absinthe rinse — smoke and anise have a natural affinity. A distinctly different drink. See Lab for direct comparison experiment.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Wine barrel finish adds dried fruit complexity that softens the austerity slightly. More contemplative than confrontational.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: In cabinet. Small pour to coat the glass — swirl and discard. The ghost of anise should be present in every sip without absinthe dominating.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Easier to integrate than a sugar cube. The sweetness is structural — just enough to round the rye's edges.

tiers.label: alternate
tiers.note: Richer and more molasses-forward. Adds a subtle caramel depth that pairs well with Røknar's smoke.

steps: Chill your coupe in the freezer while you build the drink.
Rinse the chilled coupe: add a small pour of absinthe, swirl to coat every surface, discard the excess.
Combine rye, Peychaud's, Angostura, and simple syrup in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25–30 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into the absinthe-rinsed coupe.
Express a lemon peel over the surface to release the oils — hold it close and give a firm squeeze. Discard the peel; do not drop it in.
notes: Express and discard: The lemon peel is aromatics only — the citrus oils lift the drink without the peel's bitterness sitting in the glass. This is not optional.
Peychaud's is the soul of this drink: The anise and floral quality connects the absinthe rinse to the body of the rye. Angostura alone produces a completely different drink.
Historical cognac spec: The original pre-Prohibition Sazerac used cognac, not rye. Try with Hennessy VS for a softer, fruitier, more wine-adjacent version. Equally legitimate.
Split base variation: 1 oz Rittenhouse + 1 oz Hennessy VS — splits the difference between the two historical specs. The Vieux Carré evolved from exactly this tradition.
Røknar variation: See Lab — smoked rye against absinthe rinse is specific and compelling enough to track as a deliberate experiment.
history: The Sazerac is arguably the oldest American cocktail, dating to 1830s New Orleans where Antoine Peychaud served his house bitters with Sazerac-de-Forge cognac. The drink switched to rye after phylloxera devastated French vineyards, and added the absinthe rinse as absinthe became the spirit of New Orleans culture. It's the direct ancestor of the Vieux Carré and De La Louisiane — the Peychaud's + absinthe combination that runs through The Winnequah and The Atwood traces its lineage here.

name: The Winnequah
desc: A custom original built on a rye–Islay Scotch split. Smoke and spice as co-equals, bridged by Bénédictine, deepened by Barolo Chinato, with Peychaud's and a whisper of absinthe weaving anise through without announcing it. Built specifically for this palate. Needs more reps to fully dial in — trust the stir timer.
glass: Rocks glass · Large single ice cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Big, spicy, assertive — holds its own against Laphroaig as a true co-equal. In cabinet.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Madeira, Sauternes, and Cognac cask finishes create wine and dried-fruit notes that amplify the Barolo Chinato specifically. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Phenolic, iodine, seaweed smoke — what this drink was built around. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Wilder, more aggressive smoke. Makes the drink feel less restrained. Both correct — mood decides. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The essential ingredient — bitter wine, quinine, spice. No substitute exists. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Three drops maximum — not a rinse, not a dash. Fully integrated anise whisper. If you can taste absinthe, you used too much. In cabinet.

steps: Chill your rocks glass in the freezer or fill with ice water while you build.
Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Absinthe is drops — 3 maximum.
Stir for 35–40 seconds. Trust the timer — dilution is the difference between sharp and integrated.
Drop large clear cube in chilled glass. Strain over the cube.
Express orange twist close to surface — oils on drink, not air. Run around rim. Drop in.
notes: Stir time is critical: Trust the 40-second timer. Under-stirring is the most common cause of inconsistency early on. Dilution is the difference between sharp and integrated.
Absinthe drops: 3 maximum. Use an eyedropper for precision. If you can taste the absinthe, you used too much.
Orange twist is structural: Not optional or decorative. Express close to the surface so the oils hit the drink, not the air.
Barolo Chinato is irreplaceable: Sweet vermouth doesn't work here. This drink was designed around that specific bottle.

Røknar split (pending trial): Try 1 oz Røknar + ½ oz Laphroaig instead of 1.5 oz Rittenhouse + ¾ oz Laphroaig. Triple smoke — smoked rye, Islay peat, and absinthe anise — may be extraordinary or may be too much. Worth one deliberate trial.

Cocoa bitters variation (pending): Try 1 dash Angostura Cocoa alongside or replacing regular Angostura. The chocolate depth may connect interestingly with Barolo Chinato's wine character and Laphroaig's smoke.
history: An original creation built from a palate profile — the through-lines of smoke (Laphroaig), anise (Peychaud's, absinthe), herbal depth (Bénédictine), and bitter wine complexity (Barolo Chinato) that emerged from an evening at Moody Tongue in Chicago. Named for Winnequah Road, Monona. There is no other copy of this drink.

name: The Atwood
desc: A darker, more austere companion to The Winnequah. Røknar smoked rye, Sfumato Rabarbaro, Cocchi di Torino, Bénédictine, both bitters, saline. Less smoke, more earth and root bitterness. Named for the Atwood neighborhood. First make: absolute home run.
glass: Rocks glass · Large single ice cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The house spec. Grain-forward Northern smoke pairs distinctively with Sfumato's rhubarb smoke — a double-smoke pairing confirmed as an absolute home run. In cabinet.

tiers.label: alternate
tiers.note: The canonical choice — high-proof and spicy. Fewer smoke layers but more confrontational spice. Compare to Røknar directly.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: Cask strength, confrontational spice. The Sfumato has to work harder — a more aggressive, demanding drink.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The defining ingredient — rhubarb root, smoke, and earthy bitterness. Ceiling is ½ oz — above this it overwhelms. Confirmed similar to Cynar in profile but with distinctive rhubarb smoke. In cabinet.

tiers.label: substitute
tiers.note: Artichoke-based, earthy and bitter. Valid sub when Sfumato isn't available. You lose the rhubarb smoke but keep structural bitterness.

tiers.label: variation
tiers.note: Walnut liqueur — darker and more autumnal. Deep walnut, less smoke, more bitter fruit. Worth trying in fall. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich and chocolatey — grounds the Sfumato's bitterness with wine depth. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The herbal-honey bridge. ¼ oz is precise. In cabinet.

tiers.label: variation
tiers.note: Scotch-honey liqueur — pairs naturally with a Scotch base split. Pending trial. In cabinet.

steps: Chill your rocks glass in the freezer or fill with ice water while you build.
Combine rye, Sfumato, Cocchi di Torino, Bénédictine, Peychaud's, Angostura, and saline in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 30–35 seconds — slightly longer than most stirred drinks. Sfumato needs full integration time.
Strain over a single large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Express lemon twist over the surface to release the oils, then drop it in.
notes: The Sfumato ceiling: ½ oz is the maximum — confirmed through testing. Above this dose it consumes the other ingredients.
Røknar is the house spec: Grain-forward Northern smoke + Sfumato rhubarb smoke = a distinctive double-smoke pairing. First make was an absolute home run.
Saline is essential: Three drops lifts the drink's aromatic clarity. Without it the Sfumato and Cocchi can feel muddy.

Atwood vs Winnequah: Companion originals, not variations. Winnequah is smoke-led (Laphroaig), anise-threaded, wine-complex (Barolo Chinato). Atwood is root-bitter-led (Sfumato), earthier, more austere.
Base split to explore (pending): Røknar + Amontillado Sherry (1.25/0.75 oz) — the most compelling unexplored variation. Nutty oxidative sherry against rhubarb smoke. Requires Amontillado acquisition.
Drambuie swap (pending): Replace Bénédictine with Drambuie. Scotch-honey liqueur character pairs especially well if the base is also split with Scotch.
history: A second original creation named for the Atwood neighborhood of Madison, Wisconsin. Where The Winnequah was built around the discovery of Barolo Chinato and Laphroaig, The Atwood was built around Sfumato Rabarbaro — a rare Cappelletti amaro from Trentino combining rhubarb root, alpine herbs, and distinctive smoky character unlike any other amaro. The Røknar house spec was discovered on first make and confirmed as an absolute home run.

name: Greenpoint
desc: A Manhattan riff from the Brooklyn cocktail family. Rye and sweet vermouth as the base, with yellow Chartreuse stepping in where Bénédictine sits in the Vieux Carré — adding herbal, honeyed complexity without taking over.
glass: Chilled coupe · or rocks over large cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The spice and proof are essential — the Chartreuse is assertive and a low-proof rye gets absorbed. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Wine barrel finish echoes the Chartreuse's honey notes. A richer, more integrated drink. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Honey, saffron, and 130 alpine herbs. Softer than green — the correct choice here. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich and chocolatey — holds its own alongside the Chartreuse. In cabinet.

steps: Chill your glass while you build the drink.
Combine rye, Chartreuse, sweet vermouth, and both bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds until well-chilled.
Strain into your chilled glass.
Express lemon twist over the surface to release the oils, then drop it in.
notes: Lemon over orange: The Chartreuse's herbal and honey notes are lifted by lemon in a way orange doesn't achieve.
Why it fits the wheelhouse: Structure is pure Manhattan family. Chartreuse does the same job Bénédictine does in the Vieux Carré. If you love the Vieux Carré, this lands similarly.

Røknar — skip it here: Yellow Chartreuse's honey-herbal character and smoke don't have an obvious affinity — they'd compete rather than complement. Røknar is better deployed in the Black Manhattan or Vieux Carré where the modifiers have more affinity with smoke.
history: Created by Michael McIlroy at Milk & Honey in New York City in 2006. Part of an unofficial series of Brooklyn neighborhood cocktails — each a Manhattan riff with a different modifier.

name: Mezcal Negroni
desc: The Negroni template with mezcal replacing gin. Equal parts mezcal, Campari, sweet vermouth. The smoke reframes Campari's bitterness entirely — less candy-orange, more charred and complex.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Enough smoke to anchor the Campari without dominating. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Smokier and more rustic. The drink shifts further toward your palate. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Rich and chocolatey — the chocolate note plays beautifully against mezcal's smoke. In cabinet.

steps: Combine mezcal, Campari, and sweet vermouth in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain over a large single ice cube in a rocks glass.
Express orange peel over the glass, run it around the rim, and drop it in.
notes: Equal parts is the discipline: The Negroni template only works in balance.

Spicy Mezcal Negroni (pending Ancho Reyes): Replace Cocchi di Torino with Ancho Reyes. Bitter, smoky, and hot in equal measure. One of the highest-upside agave drinks to explore once Ancho Reyes is acquired.
history: The Mezcal Negroni emerged naturally as mezcal became a serious cocktail spirit in the early 2010s. The Negroni itself dates to 1919. The mezcal substitution turns out to be a better match than gin's botanicals — smoke and Campari's bitterness work beautifully together.

name: Frisco Sour
desc: Three ingredients: rye, Bénédictine, fresh lemon. Bénédictine does the work of both modifier and sweetener simultaneously. The closest thing to a pure Bénédictine showcase in cocktail form.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The spice and proof are essential — Bénédictine is sweet and herbal, and a big rye prevents this from reading as dessert. In cabinet.

steps: Combine rye, Bénédictine, and fresh lemon juice in a shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist or Luxardo cherry.
notes: Bénédictine as the star: This is the drink where you find out what Bénédictine tastes like when it's in charge. Worth making once for that reason.
Fresh lemon only: Three ingredients means nowhere to hide.
history: The Frisco Sour dates to at least the 1930s. It predates the craft cocktail era by decades and was largely forgotten until bartenders rediscovered it as a showcase for Bénédictine specifically.

name: Espresso Martini
desc: The crowd-pleaser that actually deserves its reputation when made properly. The Friends version; see notes for a spirit-forward rye variation built for your palate.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Clean and honey-forward. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Fresh espresso shaken cold produces the best foam. Pull the shot, let it cool before shaking.

tiers.label: substitute
tiers.note: Chameleon or Trader Joe's concentrate. No foam — accept that and serve anyway. Still tastes good.

tiers.label: backup
tiers.note: Brew double strength, cool completely, use 1.5 oz. Minimal foam. A Moka pot (~$30 Bialetti) solves this permanently.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: In cabinet — evaluation pending first espresso martini attempt. If it reads too sweet, replace with Mr. Black.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.bottle: Mr. Black Cold Brew Coffee Liqueur
tiers.note: Lower sugar than Kahlúa, genuinely coffee-forward. The recommended upgrade once evaluated.

tiers.label: note
tiers.note: Mr. Black has enough sweetness without additional syrup.

steps: Pull espresso and let it cool 2–3 minutes — hot espresso melts the ice too fast and dilutes the drink.
Combine vodka, espresso, coffee liqueur, and simple syrup in a shaker with ice.
Shake very hard for 15–18 seconds — more vigorous than any other drink. The foam is structural.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe. Let the foam build on top.
Garnish with three coffee beans arranged in the center of the foam. Serve immediately.
notes: The foam: Comes from espresso crema agitated by shaking. Fresh espresso = better foam. If no foam, the espresso was too old or the shake wasn't hard enough.
Cazadores evaluation: Make the drink once before buying Mr. Black. If it reads genuinely coffee-forward, it earns its place. If it reads sweet and syrupy, Mr. Black immediately.
For your palate — Rye Espresso Martini: Replace vodka with 1 oz Rittenhouse + ½ oz vodka. Use Mr. Black. Drop simple syrup entirely. Add 1 dash Angostura. Bold, bitter, coffee-driven. Spirit-forward.
No espresso machine? Moka pot (~$30, Bialetti) is the permanent fix. Makes real crema, foams well, costs almost nothing per use.
history: Created by Dick Bradsell at the Soho Brasserie in London in 1983 when a model asked for a drink that would 'wake me up and then f*** me up.' Renamed the Espresso Martini in the 1990s, revived dramatically in the 2020s to become one of the most ordered cocktails in the world.

name: Gold Rush
desc: A three-ingredient bourbon sour built on honey syrup instead of simple. The honey rounds the bourbon's edges in a way sugar doesn't. Crowd-pleasing, easy to batch, genuinely delicious. See notes for a more complex version that fits the palate.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Carry-overs in cabinet — use them up here. When finished, replace with Buffalo Trace as the standard house bourbon.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Approachable, well-priced, crowd-friendly. The right call when making these for guests.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Barr Hill is rich — dilute slightly with water to reach 3:1 ratio. In cabinet.

tiers.label: homemade
tiers.note: 3 parts honey to 1 part warm water. Stir until dissolved, cool, refrigerate up to 2 weeks.

steps: Combine bourbon, honey syrup, and fresh lemon juice in a shaker with ice.
Shake vigorously for 10–12 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
No garnish needed, though a lemon wheel is a nice touch.
notes: Batch-friendly: Pre-combine bourbon and honey syrup. Add fresh lemon when shaking to order.

For your palate — Gold Rush with depth: Add ¼ oz Bénédictine and two dashes Angostura. The Bénédictine echoes the honey's sweetness while adding herbal complexity. Barely different to make, dramatically more interesting to drink.
Rye variation: Replace bourbon with Rittenhouse. Sharper, more spirit-forward. The honey becomes a counterbalance rather than a complement.
history: Created by T.J. Siegel at Milk & Honey in New York City around 2000. Demonstrated that honey syrup makes a fundamentally better sour than simple syrup.

name: Gin & Tonic
desc: The most ordered cocktail in the world. When made with quality gin and quality tonic, simple and endlessly variable. The Friends version is classic; see notes for a mezcal-tonic variation built for your palate.
glass: Highball or large wine glass · plenty of ice

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Honey-forward and distinctive. Excellent but less classic than London Dry for guests who want a traditional G&T. In cabinet.

tiers.label: alternate
tiers.note: Juniper-forward and dry. The classic G&T gin — assertiveness holds up against tonic. Not yet in cabinet — worth adding for guests.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The gold standard for premium tonic. Real quinine, balanced bitterness.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More bitter and herbal than Indian Tonic. The correct tonic for your palate version.

steps: Fill a highball glass completely with ice — more ice means slower dilution.
Pour gin over the ice.
Pour tonic slowly down the side of the glass to preserve carbonation.
Stir gently once or twice.
Squeeze a lime wedge over the top and drop it in.
notes: Pour tonic slowly: Down the side of the glass preserves the bubbles.

For your palate — Mezcal Tonic: 1½ oz Barr Hill Gin + ½ oz Del Maguey Vida. Use Fever-Tree Aromatic Tonic. Add 2 dashes orange bitters. Garnish with grapefruit twist. The smoke plays against the tonic's quinine bitterness in a direction that's entirely your wheelhouse.
Tanqueray for guests: Worth adding to the cabinet for guests who want a more classic G&T profile than Barr Hill provides.
history: Born from the British Empire's need to get quinine into soldiers in India to prevent malaria. Quinine's bitterness was masked with gin, sugar, and lime. By the 21st century the craft tonic movement — led by Fever-Tree founding in 2004 — transformed it from a basic drink into a serious one.

name: The Black Irish
desc: An Irish whiskey Old Fashioned built around coffee liqueur and mole bitters. Single pot still Irish is your wheelhouse's near neighbor — lighter than rye but the bitter coffee modifier and mole bitters push it into familiar complex territory.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The defining single pot still expression. Rich, oily, and complex with dried fruit and spice.

tiers.label: splurge
tiers.note: More Sherry cask influence — dried fruit and walnut notes that amplify the coffee modifier.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.bottle: Mr Black Cold Brew Coffee Liqueur
tiers.note: Lower sugar than Kahlúa, genuinely coffee-forward.

steps: Combine Irish whiskey, coffee liqueur, demerara syrup, and bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain over a large ice cube.
Express orange peel and drop it in.
notes: Why single pot still Irish: Blended Irish is light and simple. Single pot still is oily, rich, and spice-forward — more in common with rye than its reputation suggests.
Coffee as modifier: This is not a dessert drink. ½ oz coffee liqueur works like Averna in a Black Manhattan — adding bitter complexity, not flavoring.
history: Treats single pot still Irish the way a Manhattan treats rye. The category was nearly extinct by the 1990s but was revived by Redbreast and a handful of distilleries who recognized it as one of the world's truly distinctive whiskey styles.

name: White Negroni
desc: A gin Negroni variant replacing Campari with Suze (French gentian bitter) and sweet vermouth with Lillet Blanc. Suze's gentian root bitterness is intensely herbal and assertive — more complex and less sweet than Campari.
glass: Chilled coupe or rocks with large ice

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: In cabinet. Honey-forward — a different character than London Dry but works here.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Juniper-forward and dry. The classic choice for this build. Worth adding to cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: French, gentian root-based, intensely bitter and earthy. Not yet in cabinet. Try it on ice alone first.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: French wine-based aperitif — lighter and more floral than sweet vermouth.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: More bitter and quinine-forward than Lillet. The whole drink gets more austere — closer to your palate profile.

steps: Combine gin, Suze, and Lillet Blanc in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 20–25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe or over a large rock.
Express lemon peel and drop in or discard.
notes: Try Suze first: Before making this drink, try a small pour of Suze on ice. The gentian root bitterness is the missing link between your amaro preferences and the gin world.
Suze not yet in cabinet: Worth sourcing. The gentian bitterness is a genuinely new flavor direction.
history: Created by Wayne Collins in France around 2001 when he couldn't find Campari and substituted Suze and Lillet Blanc. Now considered one of the most important Negroni variations.

name: The Dirty Martini (Done Right)
desc: The vodka cocktail this palate can actually get behind — not because vodka is interesting, but because olive brine and dry vermouth are. When built properly, salinity and bitterness carry the drink.
glass: Chilled coupe · No ice · Very cold

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: In cabinet. Honey-forward — slightly less neutral than Ketel One but excellent quality.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: In cabinet. Don't skip this — a Martini without vermouth is cold vodka, not a cocktail.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Buttery, mild, slightly sweet brine from Sicilian green olives. The dirty martini made with this is a fundamentally better drink.

steps: Chill your coupe in the freezer for at least 5 minutes — temperature is critical.
Combine vodka, dry vermouth, and olive brine in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 30 seconds — longer than most cocktails. Dilution and temperature are everything.
Strain into the chilled coupe.
Garnish with 2–3 Castelvetrano olives on a pick.
notes: Why this might work: The dirty martini is primarily a salt-and-bitter drink when made with quality brine and real vermouth — hits the same notes as stirred spirit-forward cocktails.
Temperature is everything: The glass must be cold, the stir must be long, and it should be consumed before it warms.
Castelvetrano specifically: Buttery, meaty olives produce more complex brine.
history: The dirty Martini dates to at least 1901. The key upgrade: quality brine from quality olives. The rest of the arguments are mostly noise.

name: The Orchard — Your Version
desc: A Black Manhattan variation built around Ski-Hi Straight Rye — a local apple-rye from a friend's orchard. The apple whispers through Averna's herbal bitterness and Amontillado's nutty depth. First make without lemon twist: very very good. Lemon twist expected to improve further.
glass: Rocks glass · Large single ice cube

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Local bottle — straight rye with apple cider. Subtle and grain-forward; apple reads as gentle sweetness rather than fruit flavor. Low proof requires a split base.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Provides the proof and spice backbone. Ski-Hi provides the orchard thread. The 1:1 split is the right ratio — try 1.25/0.75 Ski-Hi-heavy to push apple slightly more forward.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The apple note makes Averna's caramel read slightly brighter and more orchard-forward. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: The secret weapon. Nutty oxidative depth connects apple to bitter in a way that feels intentional rather than accidental. In cabinet.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Honey-herbal bridge between the apple sweetness and the amaro bitterness. In cabinet.

steps: Chill a rocks glass in the freezer or fill with ice water while you build.
Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir 30 seconds — the Amontillado needs full integration time.
Strain over a large cube in the chilled rocks glass.
Express lemon twist close to the surface — oils on the drink, not the air. Drop in. Lemon over orange; it lifts the apple note rather than obscuring it.
notes: First make result: Very very good — without lemon twist. Lemon twist expected to improve further. Strong sign.
Why lemon over orange: Orange oil obscures the apple note. Lemon oil amplifies it. Worth making side by side once you have both to confirm.
Amontillado is the key: Nutty oxidative sherry connects apple sweetness to Averna's bitterness in a way that makes the drink feel cohesive. Don't omit it.
Proof note: Ski-Hi at 70 proof needs the Rittenhouse split to hold its own. If you ever find a full-proof version of this bottle, revisit the ratio.
Ratio variation: Try 1.25 oz Ski-Hi / 0.75 oz Rittenhouse to push the apple note slightly more forward without losing structure.
history: Built around Ski-Hi Straight Rye — a local straight rye with apple cider made in collaboration with a friend's orchard and a local Minnesota distillery. The brief was a cocktail that acknowledges apple without leaning into fruit-forward sweetness. The Black Manhattan template with Amontillado as the connecting thread was the solution. First of what may become a Local series built around regional spirits.

name: The Orchard — Crowd Version
desc: A Gold Rush riff where Ski-Hi's apple character leads rather than hides. Honey and lemon frame it naturally. Approachable, crowd-pleasing, the apple is the point. Bénédictine float bridges to a more complex version.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Higher ratio here so the apple leads — this is the version where the orchard character is the point.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Proof support — less than your version so the apple stays front and center.

tiers.label: standard
tiers.note: Echoes the Ski-Hi's apple sweetness without competing. In cabinet.

tiers.label: upgrade
tiers.note: Optional — adds herbal depth without changing the drink's approachable character. Skip for the crowd; add for yourself. Same float technique as the Laphroaig in the Penicillin.

steps: Combine Ski-Hi, Rittenhouse, honey syrup, lemon juice, and saline in a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12–15 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Optional: float Bénédictine over the back of a bar spoon for added depth.
Garnish with lemon wheel.
notes: Apple leads here: More Ski-Hi than Rittenhouse — the orchard character is the point, not the background.
Bénédictine float is the upgrade path: Skip it for the crowd, add it for yourself. Same technique as the Laphroaig float in the Penicillin.
Untested: Make this after confirming your version — the crowd spec follows the same logic but the shaken format needs its own trial.
history: The crowd-friendly companion to The Orchard — your version. Same local bottle, different format. Where your version hides the apple in a spirit-forward stirred build, this one lets it lead in a honey sour format accessible to any palate.

name: The Atwood — Røknar House Spec
spec: 2 oz Røknar · ½ oz Sfumato · ½ oz Cocchi di Torino · ¼ oz Bénédictine · Peychaud's · Angostura · Saline
desc: Used Røknar Minnesota Straight Rye instead of Rittenhouse as the base. Røknar's grain-forward Northern smoke pairs distinctively with Sfumato's rhubarb smoke — a double-smoke pairing that works at the house level. Røknar is now the permanent house spec for The Atwood.
notes: Result: Absolute home run on first make. Røknar's smoked rye + Sfumato's rhubarb smoke = genuinely distinctive double-smoke pairing. Better than Rittenhouse in this specific context.

name: The Winnequah — First Make
spec: 1.5 oz Rittenhouse · ¾ oz Laphroaig 10 · ¾ oz Barolo Chinato · ¼ oz Bénédictine · Peychaud's · 3 drops Absinthe · Saline
desc: Solid on first attempt. Needs more reps — stir time and absinthe drops are the key variables causing inconsistency.
notes: Result: Solid but needs refinement. Trust the 40-second stir timer. Absinthe drops are the most sensitive variable — 3 maximum, use an eyedropper.

name: Cynar Neat — Digestif Evaluation
desc: Tried at restaurant digestif bar alongside espresso. Very close to Sfumato in profile — both earthy and bitter, Sfumato adds rhubarb smoke. Excellent at $12.
notes: Result: Buy it. Keeps coming up across multiple recipes (Black Manhattan variation, Mezcal Paloma). $12, every liquor store. The most deferred purchase in the cabinet build.

name: The Winnequah — Røknar Split
spec: 1 oz Røknar + ½ oz Laphroaig (replacing 1.5 oz Rittenhouse + ¾ oz Laphroaig) · everything else identical
desc: Triple smoke — smoked rye, Islay peat, and absinthe anise — may be extraordinary or may be too much. One deliberate trial needed.
notes: Hypothesis: Røknar's Northern grain smoke + Laphroaig's iodine peat + absinthe anise = the most smoke-forward version of this drink possible. Could be transcendent. Could be overwhelming. Worth finding out.

name: The Atwood — Amontillado Sherry Split
spec: 1.25 oz Røknar + 0.75 oz Amontillado Sherry · ½ oz Sfumato · ½ oz Cocchi di Torino · ¼ oz Bénédictine · Peychaud's · Angostura · Saline
desc: Most compelling unexplored Atwood variation. Nutty oxidative sherry against rhubarb smoke is a combination that doesn't exist anywhere else in the repertoire.
notes: Requires: Amontillado Sherry (Lustau or Tio Pepe, ~$25). Not yet in cabinet.
Hypothesis: The sherry's nutty oxidative character amplifies Cocchi di Torino's wine depth and creates a layered complexity that the straight rye version can't achieve.

name: The Atwood — Drambuie Swap
spec: Standard Atwood spec · Drambuie replacing Bénédictine · all else identical
desc: Drambuie (Scotch-honey liqueur) replaces Bénédictine's herbal sweetness with a whisky-honey character. All bottles in cabinet — low-hanging fruit.
notes: Requires: Nothing — Drambuie already in cabinet.
Hypothesis: Scotch-honey character pairs naturally with smoked rye. May create more coherent flavour through-line than Bénédictine's herbal sweetness.

name: The Winnequah — Cocoa Bitters
spec: Standard Winnequah · 1 dash Angostura Cocoa alongside or replacing regular Angostura
desc: Cocoa bitters may connect interestingly with Barolo Chinato's wine character and Laphroaig's smoke. Subtle change — worth a direct comparison pour.
notes: Requires: Nothing — Angostura Cocoa already in cabinet.
Hypothesis: Chocolate depth bridges the Barolo Chinato's wine bitterness and Laphroaig's smoke in a new direction.

name: Penicillin — Barrow Ginger Shortcut
spec: ½ oz Barrow Intense Ginger Liqueur + ¼ oz Barr Hill Honey Syrup replacing honey-ginger syrup
desc: Eliminates need to make honey-ginger syrup. More spirit-forward, potentially less sweet. All bottles in cabinet.
notes: Requires: Nothing — both bottles in cabinet.
Note: Barrow is 'intense' — may need to reduce to ¼ oz. Compare directly to syrup version on same night.

name: Mezcal Last Word
spec: ¾ oz Del Maguey Vida · ¾ oz Green Chartreuse · ¾ oz Maraska Maraschino · ¾ oz Fresh Lime
desc: Equal parts Last Word with mezcal replacing gin. All bottles in cabinet except Green Chartreuse.
notes: Requires: Green Chartreuse — not currently in cabinet. Yellow is not a substitute here.
Hypothesis: Mezcal smoke neutralises maraschino's sweetness in a way gin can't. The equal-parts discipline keeps any single ingredient from dominating.

name: Vieux Carré — Full Splurge Spec
spec: ¾ oz WhistlePig 12 Old World · ¾ oz Pierre Ferrand Ambre · ¾ oz Barolo Chinato · ¼ oz Bénédictine · Peychaud's · Angostura
desc: WhistlePig 12 wine barrel finish + Pierre Ferrand Ambre dried fruit + Barolo Chinato bitter wine depth. The highest-upside version of this drink.
notes: Requires: Pierre Ferrand Ambre (~$40). WhistlePig 12 already in cabinet.

Hypothesis: Three wine-influenced ingredients in a single drink — the Whistlepig's Madeira/Sauternes/Port finish, the Ambre's dried fruit, and the Chinato's Barolo wine base — should create remarkable layered complexity.

name: Sazerac — Røknar vs Rittenhouse Direct Comparison
spec: Make two identical Sazeracs side by side — one Rittenhouse 100, one Røknar — everything else identical
desc: Smoked rye against an absinthe rinse is a specific and compelling enough combination to warrant a deliberate side-by-side tasting rather than just a casual swap. Smoke and anise have a natural affinity — the question is whether Røknar's Northern grain smoke enhances or competes with the absinthe's herbal anise character.
notes: Requires: Nothing — both bottles in cabinet. Make both drinks on the same night.

Hypothesis: Røknar's smoke + absinthe anise will be complementary rather than competing — similar to how the Atwood's double-smoke pairing worked. If confirmed, Røknar becomes the house spec for the Sazerac as it did for the Atwood.
Method: Make Rittenhouse version first (palate baseline), rest 5 minutes, then make Røknar version. Note whether smoke amplifies or fights the absinthe rinse.

name: Spicy Mezcal Negroni
spec: 1 oz Del Maguey Vida · 1 oz Campari · 1 oz Ancho Reyes (replacing sweet vermouth)
desc: Bitter, smoky, and hot in equal measure — but fine rather than great. Too much spice and too much Campari bitterness competing simultaneously. The Negroni format asks too much of the palate at once when heat is also present.
notes: Result: Fine but not great. Ancho Reyes as a full 1 oz replacing all sweet vermouth is too much chile liqueur. Campari's assertive bitterness competes with the heat rather than complementing it.
Redirect: Spicy heat works better in the margarita format where lime and agave give the chile somewhere to land. See Spicy Smoked Margarita.
Possible salvage: Reduce Ancho Reyes to ½ oz and add ½ oz Cocchi di Torino alongside — splits the vermouth role. Untested but may resolve the balance issue.
